procedures.anestheticConsiderationsRaw:
(Procedures covered: exploratory/staging laparotomy that is not trauma-related;
excision of intra-abdominal and retroperitoneal tumors; splenectomy.)

Patients presenting for staging laparotomy typically have lymphomatous or cancerous
disorders. Apart from the primary disease, these patients are often in reasonably good
health and will not have had radiation or chemotherapy before the staging laparotomy.
Patients undergoing resection of intra-abdominal or retroperitoneal tumors vary widely
in their overall health status (e.g., progression of tumor and concomitant diseases).
Accordingly, the extent of surgery and the potential for intraoperative complications
(e.g., major vascular injury) are case-specific and highly variable. Consequently, a
thorough understanding of the patient’s pathology and close communication with the
surgical team (sometimes multidisciplinary) about planned surgical intervention are
essential to devise a compelling anesthetic management plan.”
Patients presenting for splenectomy may be divided into two groups: (a) trauma patients
(whose management is described in Trauma Surgery) and (b) a group with
myeloproliferative and other disorders resulting in hypersplenism. Patients may have
received chemotherapy and/or radiation therapy, which may affect a variety of organ
systems. It is incumbent on the anesthesiologist to be aware of the periop implications
of these adjunctive treatments.
Respiratory
Patients who have splenomegaly and other intra-
abdominal mass lesions may have a degree of
atelectasis and compromised ventilation 2° intra-
abdominal pathology: ↓ FRC → ↑ A-a gradient + ↓
PaO2. This should be evaluated by physical exam and
close evaluation of diagnostic studies. Some may
have been treated with chemotherapeutic agents
(e.g., bleomycin at a total dose >200 mg/m2) that

cause pulmonary pathology, including fibrosis. Toxic
drug effects are potentiated by smoking, XRT, and
high FiO2.
Tests: CXR, PFTs, and ABG as clinically indicated
Gastrointestinal
Prolonged diarrhea and/or vomiting can result in
electrolyte abnormalities.
Tests: electrolytes
Cardiovascular
Patients with systemic disease requiring splenectomy
may be chronically ill and have ↓ cardiovascular
reserve. Patients who have received certain
chemotherapeutic agents (e.g., doxorubicin at a dose
>550 mg/m2) may suffer from cardiotoxic side
effects that can be worsened by XRT. Manifestations
include CHF and dysrhythmias.
Tests: ECG, ECHO, and stress test as clinically
indicated
Neurologic
Patients may have neurologic deficits from receiving
certain chemotherapeutic agents (e.g., peripheral
neuropathies caused by vinblastine and cisplatin or
CNS pathology caused by 5-fluorouracil and
mithramycin). Evidence of neurologic dysfunction
should be documented in the preop evaluation.
Hematologic
Patients are likely to present with splenomegaly 2°
hematologic disease (e.g., Hodgkin disease, non-
Hodgkin lymphoma, chronic leukemia, myeloid
metaplasia, thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura,
idiopathic autoimmune hemolytic anemia, and sickle-
cell disease). Cytopenia is very common. Preop
replacement of platelets is often a consideration in
patients with severe thrombocytopenia. However,
the effectiveness of preop platelet replacement is
limited in patients with hypersplenism because
transfused platelets are mostly sequestrated by the
spleen. Myelosuppression should be anticipated in all
patients receiving active chemotherapy.
Tests: CBC
Hepatic
Some chemotherapeutic agents (e.g., methotrexate

and mithramycin) may be hepatotoxic. Evaluation of
LFTs should be considered in patients at risk.
Tests: LFTs including INR as clinically indicated
Renal
Some chemotherapeutic drugs (e.g., methotrexate
and cisplatin) are nephrotoxic, and patients may
present with impaired renal function.
Tests: BUN, creatinine, and electrolytes
Laboratory
A T&S and T&C are mandatory in all patients with
significant relevant intraoperative bleeding risk.
Other tests may be indicated based on the H&P.
Premedication
Consider midazolam 1–2 mg iv. In patients with
suspected gastrointestinal stasis, the use of full-
stomach precautions should be considered to
minimize the risk of pulmonary aspiration. Consider
placement and suctioning of an NGT before
induction.
ERAS
Check compliance with presurgical ERAS
recommendations (see above) including NPO status.
Discuss with the surgeon the possibility of a
transversus abdominis plane or thoracic epidural
block for postop pain management. Consider preop
acetaminophen 1000 mg ± gabapentin 300 mg po
with sip of water. Consider aprepitant 40 mg po with
sip of water for patients with h/o severe PONV.

Anesthetic technique
GETA ± epidural for postop analgesia or alternative regional anesthetic techniques
including paravertebral and possibly transversus abdominis plane (TAP) blocks.
However, whether TAP blocks provide meaningful opioid-sparing and analgesic effects
in abdominal surgery is uncertain. The choice of an appropriate regional anesthetic
technique can be significantly restricted by a patient’s health status (e.g., coagulopathy)
see p. 1788–1789. If postop epidural analgesia is planned, placement of catheter before
anesthetic induction is helpful to establish correct placement in the epidural space
(accomplished by injecting 1–2% lidocaine (50–100 mg) via the epidural catheter to
elicit a segmental block). The use of epidural anesthetic techniques for postoperative

pain control in patients undergoing major, nonvascular abdominal surgery has been
shown to provide superior pain control compared with IV-PCA (20–30% difference on
postoperative days 1–3). However, adequate pain control can be achieved with the use
of IV-PCA. ERAS pathways see Appendix K, p. K-1 emphasize opioid-sparing and
multimodal analgesic techniques for the management of perioperative pain. These
techniques aim at providing superior pain control while reducing the incidence of
opioid side effects including dizziness (impaired early mobilization), slow recovery of
bowl function (delayed discharge from hospital), nausea and vomiting (decreased
patient satisfaction), and potentially life-threatening events (severe respiratory
depression). Multimodal approaches include the use of regional anesthesia techniques
and nonopioid drug classes, including nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs)
acetaminophen, N-methyl-D-aspartate (NMDA) antagonists, local anesthetics, and
gabapentinoids.

on the desired segmental spread but often ranges
between 5 and 10 mL/h. Lipophilic opioids (e.g.,
fentanyl) 2 mcg/mL can effectively be given by
continuous infusion. Longer-acting hydrophilic opioids
(e.g., hydromorphone 0.1–0.4 mg or morphine 1–2 mg
for an epidural placement at the lower to midthoracic
spine) can be injected as a bolus along with the initial
bolus dose of a local anesthetic. However, hydrophilic
opioids tend to spread rostrally within the intrathecal
space and may cause sedation and respiratory
depression if dosed too aggressively. Vulnerable patients
include the elderly, patients with obstructive airway
disease, and patients suffering from obesity. The use of
epidural local anesthetics is associated with
sympatholysis, and ↓ BP has to be anticipated. Critical ↓
BP is treated with fluids iv and/or vasopressors (e.g.,
ephedrine 5–10 mg iv). In patients undergoing a surgical
procedure with a significant risk for major bleeding, it is
prudent to delay administration of epidural local
anesthetics until the critical part of surgery has been
completed. Systemic sedatives (e.g., opiates and
benzodiazepines) should be minimized, particularly in
patients receiving neuraxial opioids as they increase the
likelihood of postop respiratory depression.
Low-dose ketamine: If the placement of an epidural
catheter is not an option, the use of low-dose ketamine
provides opioid-sparing effects (30–50%), which can be
accompanied by a simultaneous ↓ of postop pain (up to
~30%). Administration of ketamine ↓ the incidence of
opioid-mediated side effects including PONV and ↓
postoperative wound hyperalgesia, which may ↓ the risk
for developing persistent pain after surgery. Adding
ketamine to a postoperative IV opioid-PCA regimen
(typically 1–2 mg per bolus) ↓ postoperative opioid use
and pain (~30%) and ↓ the incidence of PONV (~40%).
At reported doses, the risk of hallucination is not
significantly ↑’d.
Maintenance
Magnesium: The intraop use of iv Mg++ (typically 2–4 g

(cont’d)
as a bolus/infusion regimen) has some opioid-sparing
(15–30%) and modest analgesic effects (pain 10–20%).
However, it is unclear whether administration of Mg++ ↓’d
the incidence of opioid-related side effects.
Gabapentin/pregabalin: Single-dose administration of
100–300 mg pregabalin or 600–1200 mg gabapentin is a
consideration in patients not eligible for epidural
anesthesia. Pregabalin and gabapentin can provide
opioid-sparing effects (15–40%), ↓ the incidence of the
opioid-related side effects PONV and pruritus (~30%),
and exert modest analgesic effects (10–30%). However,
administration of pregabalin and gabapentin ↑’s the
incidence of sedation (20–45%), and complaints of
visual disturbance are much more likely. As such, the
perioperative use of pregabalin and gabapentin may
hamper early postop mobilization and ↑ fall risks in
vulnerable patients (e.g., the frail and elderly). Repeated
dosing of pregabalin and gabapentin within a 24-h
interval does not offer clear benefits but ↑’s the risk of
sedation. There is also no compelling evidence to
suggest that pregabalin or gabapentin will ↓ the
incidence of persistent pain after surgery.
Nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs and
acetaminophen: Perioperative administration of
nonselective NSAIDs (e.g., ketorolac 30 iv), COX2-
selective NSAIDs (e.g., 200–400 mg celecoxib po),
and/or acetaminophen (e.g., 1000 mg po) is associated
with moderate opioid-sparing effects. Overall, NSAIDs
seem to be about twice as effective (~25%) as
acetaminophen, and only NSAIDs have conclusively been
shown to ↓ opioid-mediated side effects (e.g., PONV
~30%, sedation ~40%). NSAID but not acetaminophen
can also significantly ↓ postop pain (up to ~30%). The
continued use of NSAIDs and/or acetaminophen postop
per is meaningful to sustain opioid-sparing effects and
further ↓ the incidence of opioid-related side effects.
Potential benefits of adding NSAIDs need to be balanced
against the risk of drug-related side effects, including

bleeding and renal failure. A large postmarketing study
(>10,000 patients) suggests that nonselective NSAIDs at
recommended doses (e.g., ketorolac <100 mg/d) do not
↑ the risk of surgical site bleeding or GI bleeding in
patients <65 yr and exposed for <5 d. However, in the
elderly and patients exposed >5 d, the risk of GI
bleeding is ↑’d. Several clinical trials have also reported a
small risk for surgical site bleeding. NSAIDs should not
be withheld from adults with normal preop renal
function. However, if patients are at risk for postop renal
impairment (e.g., impaired intraop renal perfusion),
NSAIDs are best avoided.
 
Intravenous lidocaine infusion: IV infusion of
lidocaine (e.g., 1.5 mg/kg bolus followed by 1–2
mg/kg/min) in abdominal surgery will modestly ↓ postop
pain and ↓ opioid consumption (10–30%), ↓ the
incidence of PONV (~20–30%), ↑ the recovery of bowel
function, ↓ the incidence of postop ileus (2–3×), and
moderately ↓ the average length of hospital stay. It is
uncertain that these befits translate to other types of
surgery. At this time, it is also uncertain whether
continuation of the infusion into the postop period
provides additional benefits (frequent monitoring of
lidocaine plasma concentrations strongly recommended).
Emergence
Most patients can be extubated at the end of surgery.
Patients undergoing extensive surgery with major fluid
shifts may require prolonged intubation until
cardiovascular stability and sufficient reduction of soft-
tissue edema (compromised airway) is achieved. Discuss
with surgeon local wound infiltration or nerve block (e.g.,
TAP block) placement or reinforcement if initially placed
>4 h ago. Consider iv acetaminophen if po dose given
>6 h ago. PONV prophylaxis should include
dexamethasone and ondansetron.

procedures.name: SPLENECTOMY
procedures.description:
Description
Through a midline abdominal or left subcostal incision or laparoscopically, the spleen
is mobilized by dividing the lateral peritoneal attachments while the spleen is retracted
medially. (Relevant anatomy is shown in Fig. 7.9-2.) Once the spleen is delivered into
the operative wound, the short gastric vessels are clamped, cut, and ligated. This can be
done with the LigaSure device. The splenic artery and vein are then exposed with care
being taken not to injure the tail of the pancreas. By keeping the splenic hilum between
the operator’s fingers and thumb, inadvertent bleeding can be controlled easily.
Accessory spleens (incidence, 15–30%) also should be looked for if the splenectomy is
being done for ITP. They are found along the cephalad and caudad edges of the pancreas
behind the stomach and in the area of the gastrohepatic ligament, greater omentum, and
the splenic hilum. All patients undergoing splenectomy should receive polyvalent
pneumococcal, meningococcal, and Haemophilus influenza vaccines.
Figure 7.9-2 Anatomic relation of the spleen to the liver, diaphragm, pancreas, colon, and kidney. The

stomach is sectioned to illustrate the anatomic relations in situ. (Reproduced with permission from
Greenfield LJ, Mulholland MW, Oldham KT, et al., eds: Surgery: Scientific Principles and Practice, 3rd
edition. Lippincott Williams & Wilkins, Philadelphia: 2001.)
Variant procedure or approaches
Following trauma, efforts at splenic salvage (splenorrhaphy) may be made, if possible,
to preserve all or part of the spleen. This may be accomplished by the use of local
hemostatic techniques (electrocoagulation, argon beam coagulator, Surgicel or Gelfoam
soaked in thrombin, microfibrillar collagen, and the use of fine sutures or mattress
sutures with Teflon felt pledgets). Recently, splenectomy has been performed
laparoscopically if the spleen is near-normal size (see Laparoscopic Splenectomy).
Usual preop diagnosis
Staging laparotomy results; trauma; immune thrombocytopenic purpura; hereditary
spherocytosis; other hereditary hemolytic anemia types; or a variety of
myeloproliferative disorders
ERAS: Preop counseling by the surgeon/anesthesiologist should include limiting
NPO duration, alcohol, and smoking cessation, review of nutritional status,
discussion of carb loading, DVT prophylaxis, postop pain management options,
physiotherapy plan, possibility of NG tube, and urinary drain postop (see Appendix
K, p. K-1).

procedures.name: EXCISION OF INTRA-ABDOMINAL AND
procedures.description:
Description
Intra-abdominal and retroperitoneal tumors, other than those of visceral origin, consist
primarily of sarcomas (liposarcoma, fibrous histiocytomas, mesenteric fibromas, and
gastrointestinal stromal tumors). They are usually approached through a long midline
incision for adequate exposure and to assess their resectability. Resection of such
lesions may require excision of adjacent or involved small bowel or large intestine or
other involved abdominal viscera. Care must be taken not to injure the ureters or major
vessels, particularly at the root of the mesentery to the small bowel. It may be prudent to
have ureteral stents placed to avoid injury to the ureters. If residual microscopic tumor
remains, intraoperative radiation therapy (IORT) may be indicated. In certain tumors
the patient may still benefit from “tumor debulking” (removing as much tumor as
possible and treating the remaining tumor with radiation and/or chemotherapy).
Operative approaches are dictated by location of tumor. Although most operative
approaches are transabdominal, some retroperitoneal tumors may be approached
retroperitoneally via oblique incision on either side of the abdomen. Some require
thoracoabdominal incisions.
Usual preop diagnosis
Intra-abdominal or peritoneal tumor

discussion of carb loading, DVT prophylaxis, postop pain management options,

physiotherapy plan, possibility of NG tube, and urinary drain postop (see Appendix
K, p. K-1).

procedures.name: DRAINAGE OF SUBPHRENIC ABSCESS
procedures.description:
Description
Abscesses may occur in subphrenic spaces, including the right subphrenic, right
subhepatic, left subphrenic, lesser sac, or bare area of the liver (Fig. 7.9-3), following
peritonitis, abdominal surgery, or trauma. It is essential to know the anatomy of these
spaces for making a correct diagnosis and for treatment. Most commonly abscesses are
drained by interventional radiology (85%), but some may require an open surgical
approach.
Drainage is accomplished by a posterior or anterior extraperitoneal approach or by a
transpleural approach, depending on location of the abscess. Lesser sac abscesses are
best approached by an anterior transperitoneal route. Abscesses in the bare area of
the liver are drained posteriorly. After the abscess is localized, the cavity is entered by
finger dissection and drained. Loculations are broken up and the cavity thoroughly
irrigated with NS or a suitable antibiotic solution. Appropriate drains are placed, and
the wound is closed in a conventional manner. Cultures are routinely obtained.
Variant procedure or approaches
Percutaneous approaches have become more popular as interventional radiologists
gain experience. This technique should be reserved for unilocular collections, where
sterile cavities are not penetrated, and a safe route is available.

Figure 7.9-3 Anatomy of subphrenic abscess. (Reproduced with permission from Baker RJ, Fischer
JE, eds: Mastery of Surgery, Vol. I, 4th edition. Lippincott Williams & Wilkins, Philadelphia: 2001.)

Subphrenic abscess

K, p. K-1).

procedures.name: INGUINAL HERNIORRHAPHY
procedures.description:
Description
Groin hernias are defects in the transverse abdominis layer, where a direct hernia
comes through the posterior wall of the inguinal canal, and an indirect hernia comes
through the internal inguinal ring (Fig. 7.9-4). Direct hernias are medial to the inferior
epigastric artery and vein, whereas indirect hernias are lateral to these vessels. Surgical
approach can be either anterior or posterior. In general, an anterior approach (Bassini,
McVay, Shouldice, or mesh repair) is used for primary repair of an indirect or direct
inguinal hernia. The Bassini repair consists of ligation of the hernia sac and suturing the
conjoint tendon to the shelving edge of Poupart ligament. McVay repair sutures the
conjoint tendon to Cooper ligament and usually is reserved for femoral inguinal hernias.
Shouldice emphasizes the closing of the transverse fascia and transversus abdominal
muscle layers. Currently, the interposing of Marlex mesh or insertion of a Marlex plug
between the conjoint tendon, the internal oblique muscle, and the inguinal ligament is
commonly used. Mesh is associated with improved outcomes and less pain. Other
modifications are indicated in special situations.
A posterior approach is used by some surgeons for the repair of femoral hernias and
recurrent inguinal hernias and for treating incarcerated and strangulated hernias. The
posterior preperitoneal approach is usually performed by suturing the transversus
abdominis arch on the superior aspect of the hernia defect to Cooper ligament and the
iliopubic tract on the inferior aspect of the defect.
The laparoscopic approach is indicated for the repair of recurrent or bilateral inguinal
hernias and utilizes a preperitoneal patch repair and results in less postop pain and an
earlier return to regular physical activity (see Laparoscopic Inguinal Hernia Repair)

Randomized studies suggest that laparoscopic repair has inferior results.
Usual preop diagnosis
Groin pain or lump
ERAS: Preop counseling by the surgeon/anesthesiologist should include limiting
NPO duration, alcohol, and smoking cessation, review of nutritional status,
discussion of carb loading, DVT prophylaxis, postop pain management options,
physiotherapy plan, possibility of NG tube, and urinary drain postop (see Appendix
K, p. K-1).
Figure 7.9-4 Inguinal anatomy. (Reproduced with permission from Scott-Conner CEH, Dawson DL:
Operative Anatomy, 2nd edition. Lippincott Williams & Wilkins, Philadelphia: 2003.)

procedures.name: FEMORAL HERNIORRHAPHY
procedures.description:
Description
The hernia sac is exposed as it exits the preperitoneal space through the femoral canal
(Fig. 7.9-5). If the hernia cannot be reduced, the possibility of strangulation needs to be
kept in mind. The peritoneal sac in most cases should be opened proximal to the femoral
canal to gain control of the intestine before it reduces itself into the peritoneal cavity. If
the bowel is ischemic, it may require resection. The repair consists of suturing the
iliopubic tract to Cooper ligament, taking care not to compromise the femoral vein
(McVay repair).
Usual preop diagnosis
Bulging of tissues over femoral canal
ERAS: Preop counseling by the surgeon/anesthesiologist should include limiting
NPO duration, alcohol, and smoking cessation, discussion of carb loading, DVT
prophylaxis, and postop pain management options. See Appendix K, p. K-1.

procedures.name: REPAIR OF INCISIONAL HERNIA
procedures.description:
Description
Incisional hernias can occur after any abdominal incision but are most common
following midline incisions. Factors leading to herniation include wound infection,
trauma, inadequate suturing, and ischemia. Following skin incision, the skin edges and
subcutaneous fat are retracted, and the dissection is carried down to the hernia defect.
The redundant hernia sac is excised, and the fascia is freed up on both sides of the
wound. Primary closure is preferred, if possible.
Variant procedure or approaches
In addition to primary repair, the latter may be reinforced by an onlay mesh prosthesis,
or the prosthesis may be used to fill the hernial defect or placed behind the muscle
layer. In the repair of incisional hernias, laparoscopic tacking of mesh is gaining in
popularity.
Usual preop diagnosis
Incisional hernia
ERAS: Preop counseling by the surgeon/anesthesiologist should include limiting
NPO duration, alcohol, and smoking cessation, discussion of carb loading, DVT
prophylaxis, and postop pain management options (see Appendix K, p. K-1).

procedures.name: REPAIR OF ABDOMINAL DEHISCENCE
procedures.description:
Description
Dehiscence implies a “splitting apart” or “bursting open” of the abdominal wall fascia.
A complete dehiscence is a separation of all layers of the abdominal wall and often is
associated with an extrusion of abdominal viscera. If incomplete, the separation of
fascial and muscular layers results in an incisional hernia or an obstruction of a
herniated loop of intestine. The earliest sign of a wound dehiscence is the presence of
serosanguineous drainage from the wound. Minimal disruptions may be treated
conservatively with occlusive dressings and an abdominal binder. Major dehiscence
requires operative repair using careful fascial closure and retention sutures.
Variant procedure or approaches
Variations in the type of closure depend on surgeon’s preference. Interrupted,
nonabsorbable sutures and skin bridges are often used.
Usual preop diagnosis
Wound dehiscence
ERAS: For elective surgery, preop counseling by the surgeon/anesthesiologist
should include limiting NPO duration, alcohol, and smoking cessation, discussion of
carb loading, DVT prophylaxis, and postop pain management options (see Appendix
K, p. K-1).

Predisposing factors for hernia often include increased abdominal pressure 2° chronic
cough, bladder outlet obstruction, constipation, pregnancy, vomiting, ↑ BMI, and acute
or chronic muscular effort. These factors should ideally be managed preop to avoid
postop recurrence. The patient population may range from premature infants to the
elderly, who have the potential for presenting with multiple medical problems.
Musculoskeletal
Pain is likely to be present in area of hernia;

planned.
Gastrointestinal
Hernias may become incarcerated, obstructed, or
strangulated, requiring emergency surgery. Fluid and
electrolyte imbalance is likely.

Consider aprepitant 40 mg po with sip of water for

Anesthetic technique
GA, regional, or local anesthesia ± iv sedation (MAC) may all be appropriate
anesthetic techniques for uncomplicated cases (e.g., without incarceration or
obstruction). GA and epidural for postop pain control may be appropriate for patients

procedures.name: BREAST BIOPSY
procedures.description:
Description
Breast biopsy and lumpectomy entail the surgical removal of breast tissue for
histopathologic examination. The term excisional biopsy is usually applied to benign
entities and implies the complete removal of the lesion in question (e.g., fibroadenoma).
The term lumpectomy is used to characterize cancerous lesions that are removed with a
rim of normal breast tissue to achieve tumor-free margins.
Breast lesions subjected to definitive open or surgical excision can be classified as
palpable or nonpalpable. Accompanying abnormal visual changes in the breast usually
denote locally advanced disease. These include edema, redness, ulceration, and brawny
discoloration of the skin with or without alterations in the contour or size of the breast.
Palpable lesions can be described as nodules or masses having distinct or indistinct
borders or subtle parenchymal thickening. Nonpalpable lesions are discovered on
routine screening mammography and MRI or diagnostic ultrasound. Microcalcifications
masses, densities, architectural distortion, and abnormal enhancement on MRI fall into
the category of potentially malignant lesions. Ultrasound can help characterize palpable

or nonpalpable lesions as cystic or solid. MRI is not a routine screening test except in
populations at high risk for developing breast cancer. It is particularly useful as an
adjunct diagnostic tool in dense breasts, to delineate the extent of cancer and identify
other occult lesions in the ipsilateral or contralateral breast.
Most patients undergoing a surgical procedure have had a prior diagnostic biopsy: fine
needle aspiration cytology, core needle biopsy, or vacuum-assisted core needle biopsy.
Hence, these results guide the extent of surgical resection. Typically, a radiologist will
place one or more percutaneous hook wires to delineate the nonpalpable lesions.
Instead of a hook wire, radioactive seeds or optical reflectors placed close to the lesion
may be used for guiding the surgeon to the desired target. These operative procedures
are referred to as image-guided or wire-localized breast biopsies or lumpectomies.
The aim of these procedures is to remove the breast tissue surrounding the wire
including the lesion and biopsy marker. Surgeons may, in some instances, use intraop
ultrasound to identify the area of interest instead. A specimen radiograph is performed
to confirm that the desired target has been excised.
Although less common, another reason for excisional biopsy is the occurrence of bloody
or pathologic nipple discharge. The underlying cause of this abnormality typically is a
benign intraductal papilloma or, infrequently, carcinoma. The surgeon inserts
progressively larger lacrimal probes into the duct with the abnormal discharge and then
injects 0.5 mL methylene blue via an ophthalmic needle to internally delineate the duct
system. In some institutions, a ductoscope may be used to explore breast ducts.
Most newly diagnosed breast cancers are invasive, but ~20–25% of newly diagnosed
breast cancers are noninvasive or ductal carcinoma in situ (DCIS). Lumpectomy is
typically offered for invasive or in situ cancers that are 5 cm or smaller. Mastectomy is
also an option (discussed below). Recently, two consensus statements have been
published 
delineating 
recommendations 
regarding 
tumor-free 
margins. 
New
technologies and contrast agents are under investigation to assess margins
intraoperatively.
Commonly, surgeons will demarcate the lumpectomy area with metal clips or insert an
interstitial tissue marker to serve as a guide for future radiation therapy planning.
Intraoperative radiation is combined in some cases with lumpectomy for small breast
cancers. Radiation is routinely administered weeks to months after surgery either using
partial breast irradiation or whole breast irradiation regimens.
Intravenous sedation/MAC and GA are most commonly used for these procedures
When lumpectomies are coupled with nodal staging operations, GA is the preferred

modality and is facilitated by using a laryngeal mask. The latter is preferred for deeper,
larger, or multiple lesions and in cases involving soft-tissue mobilization. Field blocks
or regional anesthesia may also be considered.
Usual preop diagnosis
Breast mass; nipple discharge; atypical hyperplasia; known in situ, or invasive cancer;
mammographic, sonographic, or MRI abnormalities

procedures.name: LYMPH NODE SURGERY
procedures.description:
Description
Sentinel lymph node biopsy (SLNB) is a technique applied to patients with invasive
breast cancers who are deemed to have clinically or radiologically negative lymph
nodes. SLNB is generally not done for DCIS cancer with the exception of some large
tumors or those associated with a mass on imaging. SLNB may be performed in select
patients undergoing mastectomy for DCIS where there may be some risk of discovering
an occult invasive carcinoma. Of note, SLNB is also used for patients who received
neoadjuvant chemotherapy.
Ultrasound interrogation of the axilla and biopsy of abnormal-appearing sentinel nodes
has become a routine practice. Subclinical nodal disease is often discovered among
patients without palpable adenopathy via this approach. The biopsied lymph nodes may
be marked with a clip, radioactive seed, or black ink tattoo. A localizing hook wire may
be placed to guide the surgeon to the biopsied node as well as a specimen radiograph to
verify the resection of the targeted clip.
Sentinel lymph node(s) (SLNs) are the first nodes to drain afferent lymphatics from the
breast and the region where the cancer is located and therefore are most likely to harbor
metastatic tumor cells. The confluence of lymphatic channels at the subareolar plexus of
Sappey accounts for the fact that periareolar injections are comparable to peritumoral
injections. Most frequently lymphatic channels drain to the axilla and less commonly to
the internal mammary chain or other extra-axillary sites.
The absence of metastasis on histologic examination of SLNs predicts tumor-free status
of non–sentinel lymph nodes. In the context of breast conservation and planned whole

breast radiotherapy, completion axillary node dissection can be safely avoided in
clinically negative cases with one to two positive nodes. These techniques have been
validated in institutional and multicenter studies and prospective randomized trials.
Two types of agents have been principally tested for lymphatic mapping and sentinel
node identification procedures: vital blue dyes (1% isosulfan blue or methylene blue)
and 99m-technetium–labeled sulfur colloid (TSC; unfiltered or filtered). Different
injection sites of these agents may be used: peritumoral or around biopsy cavity,
periareolar/subareolar, or in combination. Isosulfan blue (3–5 mL) is injected in the
operating room. The breast can be massaged to promote lymphatic uptake of tracers.
The surgeon should inform the anesthesiologist when injecting the dye because a
transient drop in the pulse oximeter reading of 2–5% is frequently seen, with maximal
drop occurring within 20–25 min after injection. This is artifactual due to effects of blue
dye spectral absorption, and blood oxygen remains normal. Patients’ skin may retain a
bluish hue, most noticeable in the recovery room. The urine, stool, or emesis can be
blue for up to 24 h or more (the patient needs to be advised of this prior to discharge).
Allergic reactions consisting of “blue hives” to full-blown, life-threatening anaphylaxis
have been reported following the injection of isosulfan blue dye. Methylene blue can be
used in place of isosulfan blue and has a lower incidence of allergic reactions but can
cause skin necrosis if injected undiluted intradermally.
Figure 7.10-2 A radioactive tracer or dye is injected in/around the tumor and an external probe is used
to identify the sentinel nodes.
TSC (~1–2 mCi) is usually injected in the nuclear medicine department the day of or the
day before the operative procedure. The tracer has very low radioactivity, and no

special protection is required around the patient or in handling tissue specimens.
Postinjection lymphoscintigraphy is considered optional. After induction of GA or
regional anesthesia, the operative field (chest and lymph node–bearing areas) is
surveyed with a handheld gamma probe (a slim rod, similar to a Geiger counter). The
“hot” spot(s), denoting accumulated tracer in lymph nodes, are identified (Fig. 7.10-2).
A curvilinear incision along the inferior aspect of the hair-bearing area of the axilla is
made 3–7 min after injecting the blue dye in the breast. Typically, blue afferent
lymphatics and blue nodes are identified below the clavipectoral fascia.
The combination of blue dye and TSC yields the highest sentinel node identification
rates. Some surgeons prefer to use one of these two agents alone. Sentinel node mapping
should be done with radiotracer alone in pregnant women. Of note, hard, palpable
nodes discovered during the axillary exploration are considered sentinel nodes even if
not blue or radioactive, as the lymphatic channels may be obstructed.
Sentinel nodes may be examined intraoperatively using touch-prep cytology or frozen
section to identify node-positive cases. The number of positive nodes dictates whether
the surgeon proceeds to axillary node dissection when breast-conserving surgery is
performed. In the scenario of mastectomy or when surgery is preceded by neoadjuvant
chemo or endocrine therapy, completion axillary dissection is performed if sentinel
nodes are involved.
Whenever sentinel nodes cannot be identified, a conventional level I and II axillary
dissection is indicated, although other factors may be taken into consideration
influencing this decision. These nodes lie behind and lateral to the edge of the pectoralis
minor muscle. The level III, or highest group of axillary lymph nodes, are medial to the
pectoralis minor muscle and are not routinely removed unless clinically involved. As
part of the axillary dissection, the surgeon preserves the thoracodorsal nerve (innervates
the latissimus dorsi muscle) and the long thoracic nerve (innervates the serratus anterior
muscle), as well as the blood and nerve supply to the pectoral muscles. The
intercostobrachial nerves (sensory to the upper arm) course through the axillary
contents, and its preservation usually can be accomplished, avoiding the occurrence of
permanent dysesthesias.
Lymphedema can be a consequence of axillary nodal surgery. Axillary reverse
mapping is a procedure that maps the arm draining nodes and lymphatics in the axilla of
the ipsilateral breast. Blue dye (3–5 mL) or indocyanine green (0.5–1 mL) can be used
for the procedure. The latter is visualized with the aid of an infrared camera (SPY Elite
system, Novadaq Inc.). Visualization of these structures allows the surgeon to preserve
them, unless suspicious to harbor tumor, and lessen the chances of developing

lymphedema of the arm. Of note, indocyanine green should be avoided in patients with
iodine allergies.
Usual preop diagnosis
Invasive breast cancer

patient wishes must be considered in the anesthetic plan. The suitability of local/MAC

procedures.name: MASTECTOMY ± RECONSTRUCTION
procedures.description:
Description
The treatment of invasive and in situ breast cancer has signficantly evolved. Modified
radical mastectomy refers to removal of the breast and the axillary lymph nodes. Total
mastectomy (simple mastectomy) refers to removal of the breast alone. It is done
mainly for treatment of extensive duct carcinoma in situ or prophylaxis in high-risk
patients such as those that are mutation carriers of breast cancer susceptibility genes.
Modified radical mastectomy is performed through a single elliptical incision, whereas
lumpectomy and sentinel lymph node, or axillary lymph node dissection, are normally
done through separate incisions. Postop adjuvant radiation therapy is routinely
recommended in breast-conserving surgery and is administered following the
completion of adjuvant chemotherapy.
Skin-sparing or nipple-sparing mastectomies with immediate breast reconstruction
(see below) are increasingly performed to preserve the natural appearance of the breast.
These operations are offered to women who have had a good response to neoadjuvant
therapies. During the mastectomy, the surgeon preserves the entire skin envelope,
including the nipple-areolar complex. A variety of incisions can be used, as shown in
Figure 7.10-3. Ischemic skin complications are more likely when a large skin envelope
is retained. Skin perfusion can be monitored via fluorescent-based skin angiography
using indocyanine green. Oncologic safety should not be compromised, and skin flap
thickness should be the same as for total mastectomy. Considerations of skin envelope
size or potential ischemic complications may prompt two-staged operations. Breast
reduction surgery with concomitant lumpectomy and nodal staging is one approach to
downsize the skin envelope. In other cases, where obesity and breast ptosis are
indicators of ischemic complications, devascularization of the central breast skin,
primarily the nipple-areolar complex, is used to stimulate collateral circulation and
lessen the likelihood of nipple or skin necrosis with second-stage completion
mastectomy. The placement of incisions is radial-lateral, inframammary fold, or vertical
in lower half of the breast. Sometimes, they may be extended around part of the areolar
edge.

Figure 7.10-3 Examples of skin and nipple-sparring incisions.
Postmastectomy reconstruction is an option for most women undergoing mastectomy.
Patients undergoing mastectomy are generally presented with two options for breast
reconstruction, that is, implant-based versus autologous reconstruction. Additionally,
the issue of timing is discussed, that is, immediate versus delayed reconstruction.
Today, most women opting for postmastectomy reconstruction undergo immediate
reconstruction. The benefit of immediate reconstruction, particularly in cases of skin-
and nipple-sparing mastectomy, is that optimal reconstructive outcomes can be achieved
without the patient having to experience the psychological trauma of iatrogenic amastia.
Both reconstructive options have distinct advantages and disadvantages. Implant-based
reconstruction is characterized by technical simplicity and absent donor-site morbidity.
However, the most commonly chosen approach, that is, 2-stage expander-implant
reconstruction, necessitates a period of expansion that separates two surgical
procedures. The first stage occurs at the time of mastectomy. Here, a tissue expander is
placed either in the submuscular, subpectoral (dual-plane), or prepectoral plane. The
advantages and disadvantages of each plane are beyond the scope of this chapter. Of
note, the majority of surgeons today use acellular dermal matrices when using the dual-
plane or prepectoral approach to optimize outcomes. At the second stage, the tissue
expander is removed and the final implant, typically a silicone gel implant, is inserted.
Autologous reconstruction utilizes the patient’s tissue for breast reconstruction and as
such adheres to the time-honored principle of replacing like with like. Benefits include
the ability to recreate a natural breast ptosis as well as absence of implant-related
complications (e.g., capsular contracture, or implant malposition.). It is noteworthy that
long-term patient satisfaction has been demonstrated to be higher with autologous versus
implant-based reconstruction. The most common donor site is the abdomen. However,
alternative donor sites include the thighs and buttocks. Advances in surgical technique
have resulted in flap survival rates of 98–99% at microsurgical centers. Hence, over the
past four decades, focus has shifted away from flap survival rates and toward donor-

site morbidity. This shift is best exemplified when analyzing the various techniques that
allow transfer of abdominal tissue. While pedicled transverse rectus abdominis
myocutaneous flaps were popular in the 1980s, the development of perforator-based
techniques that spare the rectus abdominis muscle entirely (i.e., deep inferior epigastric
artery perforator [DIEP] flaps) is considered the gold standard today.
It is important to consider the effects of radiation on postoperative outcome. Radiation
is associated with a marked increase of implant-related complications, which is why
many surgeons advise against implant-based reconstruction in these cases. However,
radiotherapy following autologous reconstruction can likewise be associated with
untoward sequelae, including flap fibrosis, and volume loss. Hence, the issue of
radiation needs to be taken into account when deciding on the reconstructive plan. An
elegant approach in patients who are known to require postmastectomy radiotherapy is a
delayed immediate approach. Here, a tissue expander is placed at the time of
mastectomy. Subsequent expansion maximizes preservation of native breast skin. The
patient then proceeds with radiotherapy. Approximately 6 mo post radiotherapy, the
tissue expander is removed and autologous reconstruction performed. The key principle
is that preserving native breast skin leads to a better reconstructive outcome.
Usual preop diagnosis
Invasive or in situ breast cancer; high-risk patients (e.g., genetic susceptibility to breast
cancer; family history of breast cancer)

procedures.anestheticConsiderationsRaw:
Invasive breast cancer is frequently treated with multiple therapies, including surgery,

radiation therapy, and chemotherapy. Patients often have received neoadjuvant therapy
(before surgery) and may include chemotherapy, hormonal therapy, or biologic therapy
to induce tumor response before surgery and enable breast conservation. Less than 5%
of patients will have distant metastasis at time of diagnosis. In that small group,
consider implications of distant spread, typically to the lung, brain, liver, and bone.
Consider systemic effects of recent neoadjuvant therapies.
Respiratory
Respiratory compromise can be present if patient has
received XRT to the thorax as part of treatment.
Tests: Consider CXR if pulmonary Sx or signs of
disease present. Others as indicated by H&P
Cardiovascular
Cardiac toxicity may occur from chemotherapy for
breast cancer. Anthracyclines (e.g., doxorubicin at
doses >550 mg/m2) may cause significant and often
irreversible cardiomyopathy. The monoclonal
antibody trastuzumab may cause ↓ in LV function
that is usually reversible.

procedures.name: EXCISION OF THYROGLOSSAL DUCT CYST
procedures.description:
Description
Thyroglossal duct cysts typically are located in the midline at or below the hyoid bone
(Fig. 7.11-1). Differential diagnoses after initial physical exam include epidermoid
cysts or lymph nodes. Cysts should be removed because of an associated high risk of
infection with oral flora and a slight (<1%) risk of either squamous cell or papillary
thyroid cancer developing in the cyst itself. A transverse skin incision is made over the
cyst, and if the cyst was previously infected and sinus tracts through the skin are present;
the skin should be removed along with the cyst. The cyst is identified and followed
cephalad to the hyoid bone (Fig. 7.11-2). Then, the midportion of the hyoid bone is
resected to minimize recurrence. There may be many small tracts associated with the
cyst that tend to attenuate beyond the hyoid bone. The base of the tract or tracts is
resected up to the level of the floor of the mouth at the foramen cecum and ligated with
absorbable suture (Sistrunk procedure). The wound is irrigated copiously and closed
in layers. The wings of the hyoid bone are not reapproximated.
Usual preop diagnosis

Thyroglossal duct cyst

procedures.name: THYROIDECTOMY
procedures.description:
Description
Thyroidectomy is performed through a transverse neck incision (Fig. 7.11-3), usually
6–8 cm long. In the traditional approach, the platysma muscle is divided sharply, and
subplatysmal flaps are developed superiorly and inferiorly. The two large anterior
jugular veins must be avoided and are occasionally a source of blood loss, although
rarely of any hemodynamic significance. Once the flaps are adequately developed, a
spring or self-retaining retractor may be placed to expose the midline prethyroid fascia
(median raphe). This is divided in the midline to expose the strap muscles, which can
then be separated from the thyroid gland.
After the thyroid gland is exposed, resection can proceed. Resection may be total,
subtotal (lobe + isthmus ± partial remaining lobe), or lobar. Degree of resection
depends on diagnosis and may be modified based on operative findings. During this
portion of the operation, hemostasis is critical to maintain adequate visualization.
Resection of a lobe usually begins with ligation and division of the middle thyroid vein
along the midlateral aspect of the gland (Fig. 7.11-4).
The superior pole is mobilized by controlling and dividing the superior thyroid vessels
close to the thyroid capsule to avoid injury to the external branch of the superior
laryngeal nerve. As the dissection proceeds, care is taken to identify and preserve the
superior and inferior parathyroid glands. The lobe is retracted medially to expose the
tracheoesophageal groove. The recurrent laryngeal nerve (RLN) is then visualized and
traced along its entire course. Its function may be confirmed using a nerve monitor. The
gland is gently dissected away from the nerve and then mobilized off the trachea to

complete the resection. Any enlarged or suspicious lymph nodes are also excised and
sent for pathologic examination. Before closing, hemostasis is ensured and can be tested
with a Valsalva maneuver. The midline fascia and platysma are closed using absorbable
suture and the skin with a running monofilament suture. The use of drains remains
controversial and has not been shown to decrease the rate of hematoma formation.
Figure 7.11-3 Transverse incision at base of neck for thyroidectomy. (Reproduced with permission
from Baker RJ, Fischer JE: Mastery of Surgery, 4th edition. Lippincott Williams & Wilkins, Philadelphia:
2001.)

Figure 7.11-4 Vascular relationships to the thyroid gland. (Reproduced with permission from Greenfield
LJ, Mulholland MW, Oldham KT, et al., eds: Surgery: Scientific Principles and Practice, 3rd edition.
Lippincott Williams & Wilkins, Philadelphia: 2001.) Inset shows patient positioning with neck extended.
Minimally invasive techniques, such as video-assisted mini-incision or remote-access
thyroidectomy via an endoscopic, transoral, or robotic approach, have been described
but have not gained widespread use. Video-assisted thyroidectomy has been shown to
have similar rates of cure with superior voice preservation, improved cosmesis,
shortened hospitalizations, and faster patient recovery when compared with
conventional open surgery. Remote-access procedures have utilized various entry sites
to reach the thyroid, namely, the mouth, anterior chest wall, breast, axilla, and
postauricular area through a facelift incision. Remote-access surgery avoids the
presence of a cervical scar altogether while offering enhanced visualization and
dexterity as well as comparable postoperative outcomes. Limitations that have
prevented widespread adoption of these minimally invasive approaches include narrow
patient selection criteria (based on the nature, size, and extent of thyroid pathology as
well as body habitus), surgeon inexperience, lengthy operative time, and higher cost.
Intraoperative nerve monitoring (IONM) is increasingly being used as an adjunct to
identify, dissect, and confirm the function of the recurrent laryngeal nerve. Specialized
endotracheal tubes are inserted with surface electrodes contacting the luminal surface of

the vocal cords on either side. The electrodes are connected to a monitoring device that
continually senses EMG activity of the thyroarytenoid muscles. When the surgeon
stimulates the RLN using a probe wired to the monitor, the device detects the electrical
impulse from the vocal cords and sounds an audible alert, as well as a visual signal in
some systems.

(papillary, follicular, medullary, anaplastic); thyroid nodule; hyperthyroidism; Graves
disease

Hyperthyroidism may be 2° Graves disease (common), toxic multinodular goiter,
thyroid adenomas, TSH-secreting tumor (rare), or overdosage of thyroid hormone.
Common Sx are fatigue, sweating, intolerance to heat, ↑ appetite, ↑ HR, ↑ BP, ↑ pulse
pressure, ↑ T, weight loss or gain, thyroid goiter, and exophthalmos. Some older
patients exhibit apathetic thyrotoxicosis, which is often mistaken for hypothyroidism.
CHF and AF are common with these patients. Hypothyroidism may be iatrogenic or 2°
autoimmune thyroiditis. Common Sx are intolerance to cold, anorexia, fatigue, weight
gain or loss, constipation, ↓ HR, ↓ pulse pressure, ↓ DTR, ↓ T, and ↓ mentation. With
very few exceptions thyroidectomy is an elective surgery. An important aspect of the
preop visit is to ensure that the patient is in a physiologically euthyroid state (normal T,
HR, pulse pressure, reflexes). Patients presenting for thyroidectomy usually are made
euthyroid before surgery and may be taking one or more of the following medications:
propylthiouracil, methimazole, potassium iodide, glucocorticoids, or ß-blockers.
According to the 2016 American Thyroid Association Guidelines, patients undergoing
thyroid surgery for hyperthyroidism should receive oral Lugol solution (potassium
iodide, SSKI) to block iodine uptake and the secretion of thyroid hormone and should
receive a synthesis blocker (propylthiouracil or methimazole) at least 1 h before. Lugol
solution may also decrease intraoperative bleeding by decreasing vascularity of the
gland. Preoperative vitamin D and calcium supplementation are also recommended for
the risk of symptomatic hypocalcemia postoperatively.
General
Although cases have been reported describing total thyroidectomy for noneuthyroid
patients with worsening cardiac function who have failed aggressive medical therapy.

Thyroid storm
A life-threatening exacerbation of hyperthyroidism

occurring during periods of stress, which is
manifested by hyperthermia (>40°C), tachycardia,
widened pulse pressure, anxiety, altered mental
state → psychosis → coma, and myopathy
(rhabdomyolysis in 50%; severe in 4%). (Thyroid
storm has been mistaken intraop for malignant
hyperthermia, sepsis, anaphylaxis, and other
hypermetabolic reactions, e.g., neuroleptic malignant
syndrome.) Thyroid storm is most often associated
with Graves disease that has been incompletely
treated before surgery. General Rx: ↑ FiO2; fluid
resuscitation; electrolyte replacement/correction (↑
Ca++); cooling blankets; acetaminophen; maintain
diuresis (maintain euvolemia) if rhabdomyolysis;
treat precipitating event (infection, CHF, DKA,
pregnancy). Specific Rx: propylthiouracil (block
synthesis) (200–250 mg po q4h); sodium iodide
(block release; 1–2.5 g iv); steroids (mechanism

dexamethasone (4 mg iv q24h); ß-blockers (use with
caution in patients with reactive airway disease, AV
block, or CHF)—propranolol (20–120 mg po

300 mcg/kg/min). Note: Block synthesis before (1 h
is adequate) giving iodides to block release,

procedures.name: PARATHYROIDECTOMY
procedures.description:
Description
The traditional approach for primary hyperparathyroidism requires four-gland
visualization with removal of any abnormally large glands. Newer methods of
localization and confirmation of adenomas have ushered in an era of minimally invasive
parathyroid surgery. Minimally invasive techniques involve a focused operative
dissection 
via mini-incision, 
endoscopic, 
or 
robotic 
approach. 
Focused
parathyroidectomy is aided by the preop localization studies, the mainstays of which
are ultrasound and sestamibi scanning. If localization fails to identify the correct gland,
then the minimally invasive approach is converted to the standard incision, and all four
glands are explored until the diseased gland is identified.
For the standard open operation, an incision in the lower neck (Fig. 7.11-5) is made,
and the platysma is divided. Subplatysmal flaps are created superiorly and inferiorly to
allow for increased working space and to expose the prethyroid fascia. The midline
between the strap muscles is opened, exposing the thyroid gland. The superior
parathyroids are located behind the upper pole, which may be mobilized to reveal the
parathyroid. The inferior glands are located near the junction of the inferior thyroid
artery and the recurrent laryngeal nerve (Fig. 7.11-6). Hemostasis is crucial to
maintaining adequate visualization in the surgical field. In the traditional approach, all
four glands are identified and biopsied for confirmation of parathyroid tissue. Abnormal

procedures.description:
Description
Adrenalectomy can be performed by different approaches, each with its own merits.
Traditionally, the adrenal glands have been removed with an open incision through
either the transperitoneal or extraperitoneal (flank) approach (Fig. 7.11-8). With
some exceptions (see below), laparoscopic approaches are becoming the favored
methods. Indication in malignant disease or metastasis remains controversial and is
currently being evaluated. Relative contraindications include large adrenal
adenocarcinomas (>5 cm), malignant pheochromocytoma, invasive adrenal mass, large
adrenal mass (>8–10 cm), or other contraindications to abdominal laparoscopic surgery
(e.g., multiple previous abdominal surgeries). Each approach is discussed individually,
but their underlying principles remain the same. The anatomy of the retroperitoneum is
shown in Figure 7.11-7.
Open transperitoneal approach
This approach allows for easy access to both adrenals and is preferred for large tumors.

A midline or bilateral subcostal incision (Fig. 7.11-8) is used, with the patient in the
supine position. The left adrenal is accessed by incising the lateral peritoneal
attachments of the spleen. The spleen and tail of the pancreas are reflected medially,
Gerota fascia is incised, and the upper pole of the kidney is separated from the adrenal
gland. The left adrenal vein is identified arising from the renal vein and is ligated and
divided between ties or using an endovascular stapler. A combination of blunt and
sharp dissection is used to fully mobilize and resect the gland. The right gland is
exposed by retracting the liver cephalad and taking down the hepatic flexure inferiorly.
The duodenum and pancreas are rotated medially to expose the inferior vena cava
(IVC). Downward traction is placed on the right kidney, and the right adrenal vein is
identified entering the IVC. The adrenal vein is circumferentially controlled and
divided, and the gland is excised.
Open extraperitoneal approach (flank)
Before the advent of laparoscopic surgery, this approach was favored to minimize pain
and improve postop recovery of adrenalectomy through the use of a smaller incision and
by remaining extraperitoneal. In general, this approach is best used for unilateral,
smaller tumors. The patient is placed in the prone jackknife position, and a dorsal
curved flank incision is made, exposing the 12th rib. The rib is resected, Gerota fascia
is identified and incised, and the adrenal gland is removed.

Figure 7.11-7 Anatomic relationships of the adrenal glands. Note the origins of the three main arteries:
inferior phrenic, aortic, and renal branches. Note also the single draining veins (except for a small
accessory right adrenal vein): the right-located superior and medial and the left-found inferior and medial.
(Ao, aorta; Ce, celiac; LAd, left adrenal gland; RAd, right adrenal gland; SMA, superior mesenteric
artery.) (Reproduced with permission from Baker RJ, Fischer JE: Mastery of Surgery, 4th edition.
Lippincott Williams & Wilkins, Philadelphia: 2001.)
Laparoscopic anterior transperitoneal approach
This approach may be used for bilateral adrenalectomy with the patient in the supine
position. The surgical plan is similar to that of the transabdominal open approach but is
associated with longer operating times and additional trocar sites for placement of more
retractors to mobilize the intra-abdominal organs.
Laparoscopic lateral transperitoneal approach
This is the preferred approach for adrenalectomy in most centers. The patient is
positioned in the lateral decubitus position with the operative site up and is
immobilized with a carefully placed beanbag to minimize nerve compression injuries.
The patient is prepped for either an open or laparoscopic approach (so that conversion

to an open procedure may be done swiftly, if necessary). When adrenal glands are
removed, the right is done because there is a higher risk of converting to an open
procedure due to the proximity of the adrenal vein to the IVC.
For right adrenalectomy, pneumoperitoneum is established, and four ports are inserted
several fingerbreadths below the costal margin between the mid abdomen and
midaxillary line (Fig. 7.11-9). Attachments to the right lobe of the liver are divided, and
the liver is reflected medially to bring the adrenal and IVC into view. The
retroperitoneum is incised too close to the IVC to expose the right adrenal vein, which
is carefully isolated, clipped, and divided. Dissection of the gland then proceeds out
laterally and up superiorly using a laparoscopic energy device. Once fully mobilized,
the gland is removed through a laparoscopic retrieval bag.
The left adrenal gland is approached similarly. After placement of the trocars, the
lateral splenic attachments are incised, and the spleen and tail of the pancreas are
rotated medially to expose the anterior surface of the kidney (Fig. 7.11-10); the inferior
and medial edges of the gland are mobilized first, allowing for the left adrenal vein to
be identified. After the vein is controlled, the remaining gland is dissected free, and the
gland is withdrawn.

Figure 7.11-8 Potential incisions for adrenalectomy. (Reproduced with permission from Baker RJ,
Fischer JE: Mastery of Surgery, 4th edition. Lippincott Williams & Wilkins, Philadelphia: 2001.)
Laparoscopic retroperitoneal approach
This technique is particularly good for patients who have undergone previous
abdominal surgery as it avoids the peritoneal cavity and adhesions altogether. The
patient is intubated on the stretcher and positioned prone on the operating table with
slight flexion at the hips and knees. Bolsters are placed under the hips and chest to
allow space for the abdomen and pannus. Three ports are placed horizontally below the
costal margin into the retroperitoneal space. The posterior retroperitoneal plane is
developed, separating perinephric and periadrenal fat away from the peritoneum and
paraspinous muscles. The inferior border of the adrenal is divided from the superior
pole of the kidney, which is rotated inferiorly and medially to help expose the adrenal
vein. Medial dissection of the adrenal gland from the paraspinous muscles will reveal
the inferior phrenic vein on the left and IVC on the right. These structures further
facilitate identification of the adrenal vein, which is ligated and divided with clips or an
energy sealant device. Once controlled, the adrenal gland is separated from the filmy
attachments to the peritoneum and removed via an extraction bag.

Figure 7.11-9 Port placement for laparoscopic right adrenalectomy. Relevant anatomy is displayed
through the right lobe of the liver. (Reproduced with permission from Baker RJ, Fischer JE: Mastery of
Surgery, 4th edition. Lippincott Williams & Wilkins, Philadelphia: 2001.)

Figure 7.11-10 Exposure of left adrenal after mobilization of the spleen. (Reproduced with permission
from Baker RJ, Fischer JE: Mastery of Surgery, 4th edition. Lippincott Williams & Wilkins, Philadelphia:
2001.)
Robot-assisted approach
B o t h robotic transperitoneal and retroperitoneal adrenalectomy have been
described. Advantages of the robot include a three-dimensional view of the operative
field, superior ergonomics, and a stable camera platform. Although patient outcomes
have been comparable to that of laparoscopic adrenalectomy, training and cost are
significant drawbacks to the approach.
Usual preop diagnosis
Functioning adrenal tumors (i.e., aldosteronoma, pheochromocytoma, cortisol-
producing adrenal tumor); nonfunctioning adrenal lesions (i.e., incidentaloma,
angiomyolipoma); and solitary adrenal metastasis with otherwise negative metastatic

survey, adrenocortical carcinoma.
ERAS: Preop counseling by the surgeon/anesthesiologist should include limiting NPO
duration, alcohol, and smoking cessation, review of nutritional status, discussion of carb
loading, DVT prophylaxis, and postop pain management options. See Appendix K, p. K-
1.

Cushing syndrome
Hyperadrenocorticism can be due to adrenal hyperplasia, adrenal carcinoma, pituitary
hypersecretion (Cushing disease), hypersecretion from exogenous tumor, or exogenous
steroid administration (most common). Adrenalectomy is the traditional treatment for
hyperadrenocorticism 2° adrenal carcinoma. These typically moon-faced patients
present with one or more of the following: HTN 2° glucocorticoids, renin (usually not
severe); renal calculi; osteoporosis; glucose intolerance; personality changes; and
myopathy. In addition, a fragile vasculature predisposes these patients to easy bruising
and difficult vascular access.

procedures.name: PHEOCHROMOCYTOMA
procedures.description:
Pheochromocytoma

Tumors of chromaffin tissue origin release massive amounts of catecholamines
(norepinephrine > epinephrine) and are responsible for the patient’s clinical
presentation. The tumor is usually found unilaterally in one of the adrenal glands but
also can be found anywhere in the body that chromaffin tissue arises (e.g., urinary
bladder, sympathetic chain). There is an increased incidence of pheochromocytoma in
certain inherited diseases (multiple endocrine neoplasia type II, neurofibromatosis type
I, tuberous sclerosis, Sturge-Weber syndrome, von Hippel-Lindau disease) and with
specific gene mutations involving mitochondrial succinate dehydrogenase SDH (B, C, D
subtypes). These patients require extensive preop evaluation for cardiac injury
(myocarditis, cardiomyopathy, arrhythmias) and preparation, consisting of α-blockade
(phenoxybenzamine 10–400 mg/d). Ideally, this care should be monitored closely by the
anesthesiologist/intensivist who can provide the preoperative, intraoperative
management, and intensive care as needed.
In contrast to its use in essential HTN, ß-blockade is not indicated to control
hypertension in patients with pheochromocytoma and is dangerous when used alone.
Alone, ß-blockade may cause marked hypertension, ↓ CO, intense vasoconstriction →
CHF, 
organ 
ischemia, 
and 
shock 
(unopposed 
α-agonism). 
Patients 
with
tachydysrhythmias may require ß-blockade to control persistent reflex tachycardia but
only after institution of α-blockers. Titration of adrenergic blockade may take 2–8 wk
and should be titrated to relief of all episodic symptoms (HAs, sweating, palpitations)
and control of blood pressure. Patients should receive effective α-blocker dose for 1–2
wk before surgery. Inadequate preop preparation will increase the perioperative
morbidity of patients with pheochromocytomas. The adequacy of medical therapy is
assessed by the absence of symptoms of catecholamine excess and BP in the normal
range measured multiple times/day. The point of delaying surgery for several weeks is
to allow recovery, recovery from catecholamine-induced ECG changes, myocarditis,
and cardiomyopathy and recovery from other organ injuries (brain, kidney, and bowel)
caused by ischemia. These patients may also need recovery time to reset abnormal shifts
in autoregulation. All of these “recovery” events are considered essential to enable the
patient to tolerate surgery and the post-tumor removal shock period.
Anticipate that some degree of postural hypotension will be observed during titration of
phenoxybenzamine, and patients should be educated to avoid sudden postural
movements. There is no rush to surgery.
Respiratory
Cardiogenic pulmonary edema
Cardiovascular
Paroxysmal/continuous HTN, tachydysrhythmias,
orthostatic hypotension, hypovolemia, myocardial

dysfunction, cardiomyopathy, ventricular ectopy, ↓

(cardiac)-receptors to normal levels of
catecholamines, CHF and acute myocarditis.

and r/o cardiomyopathy (hypertrophic, takotsubo, or

as appropriate

replacement if bilateral adrenalectomy is

of water. Consider aprepitant 40 mg po with sip of

Anesthetic technique
GETA: Establish invasive hemodynamic monitoring (arterial and PA lines) BEFORE
to induction using iv fentanyl (50–200 mcg) and generous local anesthesia. These
procedures are not difficult and can be done safely with ultrasound. This not only

establishes the patient’s true hemodynamic baseline but also, equally important, allows
the anesthesiologist to pay full attention to the patient at the start of anesthesia/surgery,
rather than being distracted with placing invasive lines after induction. Femoral or
axillary arterial pressure monitoring is preferred over radial artery because of the need
to monitor “central” arterial pressures in a patient who may experience high
catecholamine levels during surgery with intense vasoconstriction. The use of a PA
catheter with continuous CO and SvO2 delivers valuable “hands-free” information
during the case. If postop epidural analgesia is planned (open surgical procedures),
placement of catheter before anesthetic induction helps establish correct placement in
the epidural space and ensuring a bilateral block (accomplished by placing 5–7 mL of
2% lidocaine without epinephrine) via the epidural and eliciting a segmental block.
Administering epidural narcotic (hydromorphone 0.4–1.0 mg) before skin incision will
enhance preemptive analgesia effect if lidocaine test dose is not used. Epidural
catheters cannot be used for a posterior approach because they are in the operative
field. Epidurals are not indicated for laparoscopic procedures.
Epidurals block neurally mediated sympathetic responses which are amplified by
sympathetic nerve endings that are supersaturated with catecholamines and may → ↓
tumor release of catecholamines but do not block catecholamine release resulting from
direct surgical manipulation of tumor. Local anesthetic-induced sympathetic block after
tumor resection may compound ↓ BP at this important stage in the operation. If the
patient’s BP is stable at the time of skin closure and is not on vasopressors, the epidural
can be bolused with long-acting local anesthetic to allow for a comfortable emergence.
Induction
Gentle iv induction (titration to effect with propofol)
and muscle relaxation (vecuronium 0.1 mg/kg or
rocuronium 0.8 mg/kg). Deep mask GA before
laryngoscopy. Double DL with LTA spray (4%
lidocaine, 4 mL) will minimize the response to
intubation.
ERAS
Verify preincision antibiotics. Assess volume status
(see Appendix K). Maintain normovolemia and
normothermia. Consider preincision placement of
nerve blocks.
Maintenance
Volatile anesthetic (isoflurane, sevoflurane), opiate
(hydromorphone), and muscle relaxant. Most
patients who undergo laparoscopic surgery can be
extubated at the end of the case, so use of sedatives

(opiates, and benzodiazepines. etc.) should be
minimized during this type of anesthetic to avoid
postop respiratory depression.

procedures.name: KIDNEY TRANSPLANTATION: CADAVERIC AND
procedures.description:
Description
Kidney transplantation offers patients with end-stage renal disease (ESRD) freedom
from dialysis. The source of the renal graft may be a deceased donor, a relative (e.g.,
parent, sibling), or a genetically unrelated donor such as a spouse, friend, or person
through paired donor exchange.
After induction of anesthesia, a 3-way Foley catheter is placed into the bladder. The

kidney allograft is placed in the extraperitoneal iliac fossa. A curvilinear incision is
made in the right or left lower quadrant. The retroperitoneal space is developed by
retracting the peritoneum medially and cephalad, exposing the iliac vessels. A self-
retaining retractor is placed to maintain exposure. The lymphatics surrounding the
external iliac artery and vein are ligated and divided. Several centimeters of the vessels
are mobilized.
The external iliac vein is clamped first, and the renal vein-to-iliac vein anastomosis is
performed. When a right deceased donor kidney is used, the renal vein will often have
been extended using the donor cava, since the right renal vein is often quite short. Then,
the external iliac artery is clamped, and a renal artery-to-iliac artery anastomosis is
performed. Usually, deceased donor kidneys will come with a “Carrel” patch of the
aorta to allow for a larger anastomosis. The living donors do not have the patch and
therefore have a smaller arterial anastomosis. The patient should be euvolemic at this
point; mannitol and/or furosemide can be given. The clamps are then released starting
with the renal vein (Fig. 7.12-1).
The bladder is filled with an antibiotic irrigation solution to facilitate its identification
and exposure for the implantation of the ureter. The spatulated ureter is anastomosed to
the mucosa of the bladder with fine monofilament absorbable sutures, often over a stent.
The detrusor muscle is then reapproximated over 3–4 cm of the ureter to create an
antireflux valve. The wound is closed, normally leaving native kidneys intact. Many
surgeons will leave a closed-suction drain around the kidney.

Figure 7.12-1 Sketch of a kidney transplant labeled 1, 2, 3 in the order of the surgical anastomoses. 1,
renal vein to external iliac vein; 2, renal artery to external iliac artery, and 3, ureter to bladder. The inset
shows the lower quadrant curvilinear incision (Paul Gallo, DDS).

Cadaveric or live-donor transplantation
Usual preop diagnosis

procedures.name: CADAVERIC KIDNEY/PANCREAS
procedures.description:
Description
Pancreas transplantation: Combined kidney and pancreas transplantation not only
provides renal replacement for type I diabetes patient with ESRD but also controls
diabetes. Over 80% or more of pancreas transplants are performed in combination with
kidney transplantation from the same donor (simultaneous pancreas-kidney [SPK]
transplant). Pancreas transplantation also can be performed for patients who have
already received a kidney transplant (pancreas after kidney [PAK]). Less commonly,
pancreas transplantation is done for patients with brittle diabetes or with impending
complications while they still enjoy normal or near-normal kidney function.
Immunosuppression regimen for pancreas transplantation is generally more aggressive
than that used for kidney transplantation, and induction therapy with antilymphocyte
preparation (ATG, IL-2 blockers) is commonly used.
The pancreas transplant is placed in the right iliac fossa, and the kidney transplant is
placed in the left iliac fossa. This can be done through a transperitoneal lower midline
incision or through two separate extraperitoneal lower quadrant incisions in the same
manner as kidney transplantation. The graft is first prepared on the back table. For
arterial inflow, a Y-graft is fashioned using the donor iliac artery bifurcation to provide
circulation to both the superior mesenteric and the pancreatic artery. The portal vein
coming off the pancreatic graft is anastomosed to the external iliac vein. The Y
extension arterial graft is then anastomosed to the recipient external or common iliac
artery. The donor duodenum is anastomosed to a loop of small bowel or to the urinary
bladder to drain the exocrine secretions (Fig. 7.12-2A). With pancreas transplantation,
there may be significant blood loss if the graft mesenteric vessels are not occluded
properly. After the pancreas is implanted, the kidney transplant is placed into the
opposite iliac fossa (as described in Kidney Transplantation).
Variant procedure or approaches
The pancreas may be placed in the upper abdomen with the portal vein anastomosed to
the superior mesenteric vein. The exocrine secretions are bowel-drained. This more
physiologic approach, however, is associated with a higher technical failure rate and
requires a long upper midline incision (Fig. 7.12-10). Pancreatic islet cells may be
infused via a radiologic portal vein approach, a procedure that is usually performed in
the radiology/angiography suite.
Usual preoperative diagnosis
ESRD 2° diabetes mellitus (DM)

ERAS: Preop counseling by the surgeon/anesthesiologist should include limiting
NPO duration, alcohol and smoking cessation, review of nutritional status and
preop supplementation, discussion of carb loading, DVT prophylaxis, urinary drain,
pain management options, and postop recovery plan. See Appendix K, p. K-1.
Figure 7.12-2 A: SPK transplantation, with drainage of pancreatic exocrine secretions into the bladder.
Note that portal vein drains into iliac vein (systemic venous [SV] drainage). In normal individuals, 50% of
secreted insulin is extracted from the circulation in the first pass through the liver. Transplant recipients
with SV have peripheral insulin levels 2–2½ × higher than normal. B: SPK transplantation with drainage
of pancreatic exocrine secretions into the proximal jejunum (enteric drainage [ED]). This technique has
been adopted for SPK by most transplant centers in the United States for solitary pancreas
transplantation; most centers still utilize ED to allow monitoring of the urinary amylase. Note that donor
portal vein drains into the recipient superior mesenteric vein (portal venous [PV] drainage) preventing
peripheral hyperinsulinemia. Most centers continue to place the pancreas in the pelvis, combining ED and
SV, which requires enteric anastomosis to a more distal segment of the jejunum or ilium. (Reproduced
with permission from Greenfield LJ, Mulholland MW, Oldham KT, et al., eds: Surgery: Scientific
Principles and Practice, 3rd edition. Lippincott Williams & Wilkins, Philadelphia: 2001.)
